<reason>CON (Side A) built a sharper, more concrete case by exploiting specific equity harms (rural students, disabled students, scheduling-constrained students) that a categorical "physical/arts before digital" rule would create, and it converted PRO's own equity framing into an argument against PRO. Crucially, CON introduced a clear alternative decision rule—match remedy to specific unmet need rather than freeze by category—which directly answered PRO's own pressure question about children being perpetually deprioritized, and which PRO never fully dislodged. PRO's rebuttals restated the "categories provide distinct, non-substitutable value" theme across rounds without adequately explaining why a ready, need-matched digital option must wait behind an unrelated physical-access project, and PRO's late attempt to flag inconsistency in CON's "finite budget" language (closing) was a fair point but arrived too late and under-developed to overturn the triage framework. Both sides executed the Pressure Questions format properly with A1/A2 labels, but CON's answers were more concrete and decisive, while PRO's were serviceable but softer ("no universal number of weeks"). Overall CON gave the cleaner, more defensible path to negate the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 clarification (A4.3) that its triage rule "matches remedy to specific unmet need, using speed only among options that can meet that need" directly answered PRO's Pressure Question about excluded children being perpetually deprioritized, and PRO's Rebuttal 2/closing response never squarely dislodged this reframe, leaving CON's alternative sequencing principle as the more resolved account of how priorities should actually be set.</best_rebuttal>
